Recovery Bridge: setup and run

Version 2.0 · 12 October 2026 · Research prototype · Synthetic data only

Recovery Bridge supports recovery planning and discharge coordination for inpatient alcohol care staff. It does not make clinical decisions or connect to clinical systems.

Open the GitHub Pages prototype

Use the supplied GitHub Pages application link. The published demonstration site is public. A normal modern desktop or tablet browser is sufficient. The first visit loads six fictional ACTS referrals; no sign-up or patient details are required inside the prototype. No ChatGPT sign-in is required. The demonstration staff selector is a viewpoint control, not authentication.

Run a local copy

Download Source & documentation from Guide & research, then extract the ZIP into a new folder. The archive includes dist/, docs/, tests/, package.json, README.md and this guide. It excludes hosting identity, credentials and Git internals.

With Python 3 installed, run this from the extracted folder:

python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory dist

Open http://localhost:8000. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. Serve over HTTP; opening index.html directly as a file is not supported because it uses JavaScript modules. Alternatively, with Node.js and npm installed, use npm start (this also needs Python 3).

To run the automated checks, use Node.js 22 or later:

node --test tests/*.test.mjs

No dependency installation, API key, database, cloud account or build step is needed for local use. The hosted instance and local copy have separate browser storage because they have different origins.

Stack and structure

The prototype uses semantic HTML, CSS and browser-native JavaScript modules. Keeping a local-only application buildless reduces setup cost and avoids unnecessary backend dependencies. Domain rules, seed data and UI logic are separated:

File Responsibility
dist/index.html Document, application root, feedback region and native dialog
dist/styles.css Responsive interface, focus styles, status labels and print layout
dist/data.mjs Six synthetic scenarios, five demonstration staff and fictional directory
dist/core.mjs Filters, counts, status rules, validators, storage and handover generation
dist/journey.mjs Treatment timeline, milestones, event validation and recorded plan updates
dist/app.mjs Rendering, forms, navigation and interaction handlers
dist/research.html Separate human-readable research and implementation pack
tests/ Domain and event-handler tests; no browser engine

Persistence and reset

Saved forms write a versioned JSON object to the browser's local storage, under recovery-bridge-v2. Changes survive refreshes on that browser and origin. Unsaved form edits are discarded on Cancel; handover preview edits require Save edited draft. A successful save message follows a completed storage write. A failed write leaves the previous saved state unchanged.

Demo settings can export the current synthetic dataset as JSON. The JSON export is a backup for inspection, not an implemented import workflow. Reset demonstration data restores the original six ACTS referrals, checklist, staff viewpoint and fixed reference date. Reset requires an explicit in-app confirmation because it discards local edits.

If saved data is unreadable, the prototype displays a warning and blocks new saves until reset; it does not silently replace the unreadable data.

The reference date is initially 12 October 2026. Overdue means due before that date, rather than before the computer's current date. Change it in Demo settings if needed. Completion timestamps use the computer's actual clock and display Europe/London time.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Check
Blank local page Serve dist/ over HTTP; ensure all four .mjs files and styles.css were extracted.
Changes do not persist Enable browser storage; avoid private browsing for retained evaluation sessions. Read the save feedback.
No rows after filtering Clear filters. ACTS referrals without a discharge date cannot match a discharge date range.
Cannot confirm a referral or follow-up Review the form validation. A confirmed arrangement needs its actual contact details.
Counts differ from the baseline Clear all filters, restore the demonstration date, or reset local scenario edits.

There is no multi-user database, real-time synchronisation or concurrent-edit protection. Use a single browser tab per evaluation participant.

Publish with GitHub Pages

The repository includes .github/workflows/pages.yml. In repository Settings → Pages, select GitHub Actions as the source. Push to main or run the Test and deploy GitHub Pages workflow manually. It tests the application and publishes only dist/, with no build step or deployment secret. The published URL is reported by the deployment job. A standard public repository and the included github.io address support the free route.

The workflow uses standard Ubuntu runners; no Codespaces, larger runners, custom domain or paid add-on is required. GitHub Pages has usage limits; this small research demo is designed for modest evaluation traffic. Exact pricing and limits should be checked before changing the hosting configuration.

Primary references: Pages availability, custom workflows, and Actions billing. Checked 12 October 2026.

Version 2 referral migration

The primary record is now an ACTS referral, representing one treatment journey, including post-discharge ACTS contact. Onward referrals are separate linked records. Version 1 browser-local plans are migrated when opened: goals, actions, community referrals and follow-up are retained. The former identifier remains stable. Receipt dates and historical clinical events remain blank because they cannot be inferred. The original recovery-bridge-v1 storage is retained as a backup; subsequent saves use recovery-bridge-v2. Reset is optional and restores the new six synthetic journeys.

Use Demo settings → Reset demonstration data to explore the new timeline examples after exporting any synthetic edits you want to keep. Each browser has its own data; opening this URL on another computer starts a separate demonstration.

Recovery Bridge: ACTS staff user guide

Version 2.0 · Fictional scenarios only. Do not enter real patient information.

Open the referral register

The main record is a referral into the Addictions Team (ACTS). Each referral follows one fictional person's treatment journey, including ACTS follow-up after hospital discharge. A subsequent ACTS referral can be created as a separate journey; the prototype has no cross-referral patient index.

Search by referral identifier, fictional name, reason, goal, action or treatment event. Filter by journey status, site, ward, assigned practitioner, planned discharge date and action status. The default view shows open journeys: Awaiting assessment, Active treatment and Follow-up. Choose All journeys or Closed to retrieve earlier journeys. My referrals filters by the selected demonstration practitioner; it is not authentication.

Select an attention count to filter the same records used to calculate the counts. The ACTS referrals card clears the attention filter. All demonstration staff views can edit synthetic records.

Create or edit an ACTS referral

Choose New ACTS referral. Record the fictional patient label, received date and optional time, referral route, reason, assigned ACTS practitioner, location and journey status. Add planned discharge when known. Dates can remain missing and are labelled Not recorded. Edit referral updates these fields. Journey status is staff controlled; closing it does not complete actions or prove clinical clearance.

Record the treatment journey

The Treatment journey tab opens by default. Its milestone cards summarise recorded evidence for referral, assessment, treatment/support, discharge and follow-up. They are not clinical progress scores. A planned assessment remains Planned until its actual outcome is recorded.

Choose Add treatment event for triage, initial contact, initial/full assessment, review, detox start/end, recovery planning, support intervention, onward referral activity, discharge planning/discharge, follow-up, journey closure or another event. Enter a brief title, event date, optional time, status, practitioner, method/location, notes, outcome and next action. Contact duration and a previously assessed AUDIT score are optional; the app generates no interpretation or treatment recommendation.

A Completed, Planned or Not completed event requires a date. Completed and Not completed events cannot be after the demonstration date or before a known ACTS referral date. Planned events may have future dates. A passed planned date is flagged for review and is never automatically completed.

Summary view shows the full chronological list with brief context, status and practitioner. Detailed view shows contact details, notes, outcome, next action and recording timestamps. Both views use the same events. Filter by event type/status and select earliest or latest first. Undated entries remain visible at the end.

Changes to goals, support, barriers, actions, onward referrals, follow-up or referral metadata also appear as Record updates. These show the save time and demonstration account, not the clinical occurrence date or an authenticated author. Select Treatment events to focus on contacts and milestones. Editing a treatment event updates that event; this is not an immutable audit log.

Recovery and discharge coordination

Under Recovery support, record the person's goals, preferences, resources, review and relevant barriers. Support discussion, offer, decision and arrangement are independent: Discussed, Offered, Accepted and Arranged are different stages. Keep declined decisions visible.

Under Discharge actions, add tasks or choose relevant example checklist items. Assign owners and due dates. Complete records a timestamp; Reopen restores Pending and clears its current completion timestamp. Missing owners/dates remain visible. Declined and Not applicable are distinct from Completed.

Under Onward support, track referrals ACTS makes to other fictional services. These are separate from the original ACTS referral. Record preparation, submission, acceptance, consent, response and next action. Submission does not demonstrate engagement. Record follow-up separately; confirmation requires date, method, details and practitioner. No referral is transmitted.

Review and share the handover

Handover generates an editable preview with the ACTS referral details and dated treatment journey, recovery goals/preferences, agreed support, actions/owners, onward referral status, follow-up and unresolved barriers. Missing information stays visible. Save edited draft before leaving. Print/save as PDF or Export text uses the preview. When source details change, the preview refreshes rather than reusing a stale draft. Nothing is sent to a service.

Count definitions

Label Definition
ACTS referrals Records matching all current filters; the scope also states how many are open
Assessment to record Open journeys without a Completed initial or full assessment event
Outstanding Action status Not recorded, Pending or In progress
Overdue Outstanding action with a due date before the demonstration date
Unassigned Outstanding action without an owner
Onward response pending Onward referral status Submitted
Follow-up to confirm Follow-up arrangement status Pending or Not recorded

Empty sections do not create fabricated tasks or pending referrals. The workspace and handover explicitly show the gaps.

Saving and keyboard use

Forms save using their Save button. Successful feedback follows the storage write. Changes persist across refreshes in this browser only. Other computers have separate data. One tab per participant is recommended.

Tab and Shift+Tab move through controls. Enter/Space activate buttons. Arrow keys, Home and End navigate the five workspace tabs. Native modal forms support Escape, focus trapping and return focus. A skip link goes to main content.

Demo settings provides reusable checklist configuration, the reference date, JSON export and a confirmed reset. Saved version 1 plans are retained as ACTS referrals; earlier clinical history is not invented. Reset only if you want the new synthetic journey examples and have retained any edits you need.

Behavioural design rationale

Target behaviour: staff record a person-centred recovery plan, allocate and update coordination actions, verify referral and follow-up progress, and review a clear handover.

This is a design hypothesis for staff behaviour, not evidence of an effect on staff performance or recovery outcomes. The mapping below is an applied interpretation of Persuasive Systems Design (PSD) and COM-B, to be tested through staff evaluation. It is not a completed behavioural diagnosis of the service.

COM-B considers capability, opportunity and motivation in relation to behaviour. PSD offers design principles including reduction, tunnelling, tailoring, self-monitoring, reminders and suggestions. The prototype applies selected principles with low-pressure prompts rather than rewards or competitive feedback. [1,2]

Implemented feature Intended staff behaviour PSD interpretation COM-B hypothesis Evaluation question
One ACTS referral workspace with four sections Find context and update the plan without repeated navigation Reduction; tunnelling through a recognisable workflow Psychological capability: reduce memory demand; physical opportunity: convenient access Where did you have to search or duplicate work?
Next useful step card Review ownership gaps, overdue work, referral responses or confirmation details Suggestion; contextual reminder Psychological capability and reflective motivation: clarify the next action and its purpose Was the prompt relevant, understandable and proportionate?
Relevant checklist selection and reusable items Create a consistent action plan while excluding irrelevant items Reduction; tailoring Capability: recall planning domains; opportunity: reduce entry effort Did useful defaults save effort or encourage inappropriate copying?
Visible owner and due date; Unassigned state Allocate responsibility and coordinate with colleagues Reduction of ambiguity; social support interpretation, without comparison or pressure Social opportunity: agree responsibility and communication Could you tell who would take the next step?
Counts and labelled action progress Review unresolved coordination work Self-monitoring of the recorded plan Reflective motivation: see the remaining work; capability: interpret status Did the progress view imply clinical readiness?
Separate discussion, offer, decision and arrangement Preserve what was discussed and what the person agreed to Reduction through structured distinctions Psychological capability: avoid conflating stages Could you distinguish an offer from an arranged service?
Separate referral and follow-up records Record submission, acceptance and confirmation accurately Reduction; suggestion through validation Capability: recognise different events; opportunity: capture them at the point of work Did you assume a submitted referral meant an appointment existed?
Brief checklist explanations Understand the purpose of coordination actions Suggestion; credibility through transparent reasoning Reflective motivation: connect the task with a clear practical purpose Did the explanation help, or add clutter?
Generated handover with explicit missingness Review and share an accurate account without retyping Reduction; self-monitoring Capability and physical opportunity: lower transcription effort and expose gaps What did you correct or check before export?
Declined and not applicable remain visible Respect choices and avoid irrelevant work Tailoring; transparent system behaviour Capability: recognise different reasons for an unfinished plan Did status language feel respectful and useful?

No behavioural mechanism is presumed proven by this mapping. Verify actual barriers through interviews: lack of knowledge, time pressure, fragmented systems, unclear responsibilities or competing demands may require different interventions. Digital prompts alone cannot resolve staffing or external-service constraints.

Guardrails

Prompts appear in context and explain why the information matters. There are no pop-up reminder streams, scores, badges, streaks, leaderboards or claims of improved recovery. Missing fields remain visible rather than being auto-completed. Staff can leave sections empty, mark them not applicable or record declined support. Defaults are proposals that staff review.

The progress measure reports action completion only. Declined and not applicable actions are excluded from outstanding work but remain distinct from Completed. Completion never labels the person clinically ready for discharge.

The team-lead workload view supports allocation, not performance ranking. Role views do not impose permissions or represent authenticated users.

Sources

  1. Oinas-Kukkonen, H. & Harjumaa, M. (2009). Persuasive Systems Design: Key Issues, Process Model, and System Features. Communications of the Association for Information Systems, 24, Article 28. Publisher record.
  2. Michie, S., van Stralen, M. M. & West, R. (2011). The behaviour change wheel: a new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions. Implementation Science, 6, 42. Open-access article.

Sources checked 12 October 2026. The feature mapping is the prototype designer's interpretation and should be refined with staff findings.

ACTS referral journey design

Feature Intended staff behaviour COM-B Persuasive Systems Design Evaluation question
Referral-centred default workspace Review the ongoing ACTS journey, including post-discharge contact Psychological capability; physical opportunity Reduction; tunnelling Can staff distinguish ACTS referral, admission/discharge and onward referral?
Summary/detail timeline with shared data Orient quickly, then inspect event context when needed Psychological capability Reduction; tailoring Can staff reconstruct what happened and what is still planned without losing context?
Named event responsibility and next action Identify who should act next Social opportunity Cooperation; social facilitation Is ownership clear, including unassigned events?
Evidence-based milestone labels Distinguish recorded activity from planned or missing history Psychological capability; reflective motivation Self-monitoring; feedback Do staff understand that milestones are documentation, not clinical clearance?
Date validation and missing-history prompts Record events accurately rather than infer them Psychological capability Reminders; error prevention within reduction Can staff correct dates without unnecessary interruption?
Visible record updates with separate save times Understand changes to coordination plans without mistaking them for clinical contacts Psychological capability; social opportunity Transparency; feedback Can staff tell the event date from the recording time?

These mappings are hypotheses for evaluation, not evidence of behaviour change or recovery benefit. No gamification or clinical effectiveness claim is added.

Recovery Bridge: staff evaluation guide

Research prototype · Fictional scenarios only · Version 2.0

Aim and boundaries

Evaluate whether inpatient alcohol care staff can use the prototype to document recovery priorities, coordinate actions, distinguish referral and follow-up states, and prepare a clear handover. Assess usability, perceived acceptability, appropriateness and feasibility. Do not infer clinical effectiveness, improved recovery or real discharge safety from prototype performance.

This is a proposed study procedure, not a report of completed evaluation. No participant data or results have been collected.

Participants and session plan

Recruit staff who carry out or coordinate inpatient alcohol recovery and discharge planning. Include nurses/practitioners with varied digital confidence and, where relevant, coordinators or leads. Agree the dissertation's sampling, approvals, consent, recording and data handling with the supervisor and service before recruitment. Participation should be voluntary; individual performance should not be reported to line managers.

A practical formative round could involve 5–8 staff, followed by revision and a second small round if time permits. This is a planning assumption, not a powered effectiveness study. A purposive sample and role balance matter more than a fixed target. Record relevant work experience and digital confidence without collecting unnecessary identifiers.

Allow approximately 50–60 minutes: 5 minutes introduction, 30–35 minutes tasks, 5–10 minutes questionnaires and 10 minutes interview. Pilot timing first. Use a separate local browser profile or reset between participants; do not expose a previous participant's edited scenarios.

Keep the reference date at 12 October 2026. Use only the synthetic names and services. Do not ask staff to reconstruct a real patient case. Explain that the staff selector changes a demonstration view and that all views can edit.

Read a standard introduction: “We are testing the prototype, not your performance. Please work with these fictional scenarios and say what you are looking for or expecting. You can skip a task or stop. The tool does not make clinical decisions.”

Use task wording, not click instructions. Offer neutral encouragement; record any assistance rather than silently helping. Stop and discuss if a participant enters real information. Store research observations separately from the app, with participant codes rather than staff names.

Scenario-based tasks and expected evidence

Task given to the participant Expected outcome / observer check Important error to record
1. Find the Poole ACTS referral planned for discharge on the demo date whose community referral has not been answered. Explain what still needs checking. Identifies Robin, ACTS-DEMO-003; submitted referral, unresolved response and pending follow-up identified. Treats submission as successful engagement or confirmed follow-up.
2. Open Sam's plan. Record the fictional goal “Build a daily routine”, a preference for written information, and a review for 13 Oct 2026. Allocate the unassigned goal discussion to Daniel and mark it completed. Goal/preferences/review saved; owner Daniel; one completed action with timestamp; Sam's outstanding count falls from 2 to 1. Missing information interpreted as already completed; wrong ACTS referral or owner.
3. For Jamie, review the housing, transport and communication barriers. Assign the alternative contact-route action to Omar and record that the team will agree a written contact route. Action owner and notes saved; barriers remain visible until actually resolved. Marks housing resolved just because a referral was submitted.
4. For Robin, the fictional service has now accepted the referral. Record the response, then arrange a confirmed telephone call on 16 Oct 2026 at 14:00, owned by Morgan; the named fictional worker will call using the agreed contact route. Referral Accepted; follow-up separately Confirmed with date/time/method/details/owner; awaiting response falls by 1 and follow-up-to-confirm falls by 1. Changes one status and assumes the other automatically updated.
5. Review Casey's declined group support. Prepare a handover without converting declined support into completed or accepted support. Declined decision and written information preference preserved; no invented group appointment. Overrides the person's recorded choice or conflates Declined with Completed.
6. Create a fictional ACTS referral for Jordan received on 12 Oct 2026 from the Ward team at Poole, Demo ward, assigned to Priya, planned discharge 18 Oct 2026. Select only the recovery-goals and follow-up items from the example checklist. New record saved; two relevant Pending actions with reviewed owner/date; remaining sections explicitly missing. Copies all irrelevant checklist items or invents referral details.
7. Open Alex's handover. Check the dated discharge event, planned ACTS follow-up and confirmed community appointment; edit the preview to add “Reviewed in fictional team discussion”. Save, refresh the page, reopen Alex and export the handover as text. Draft persists unchanged across refresh; planned ACTS contact and 16 Oct 14:00 appointment still accurate; exported text matches preview. Loses edits, exports stale information, or assumes the plan proves clinical readiness.
8. Using the keyboard only, open Taylor, review the proposed follow-up and navigate to the handover. Explain why the follow-up is still pending. Core controls reachable; tab navigation and dialog behaviour usable; proposed date not interpreted as confirmed. Cannot reach a control, loses focus, or calls the proposed appointment confirmed.

Tasks 2–7 change records. Use the expected deltas within a task, not the untouched baseline totals. Reset before another participant; record the start state if task order is changed. Do not request Reset until the observer has retained any agreed synthetic evidence.

Measures and observation sheet

Record participant code, role category, task, start/end time, outcome, errors, assistance and comments. Avoid patient information and unnecessary staff identifiers. Collect recordings only if consented and approved.

Measure Definition / recording rule
Task completion Independent success, assisted success, partial completion or failure against the specified outcome
Completion rate Independent successes ÷ tasks attempted; show numerator and denominator. Report assisted successes separately.
Time on task Seconds from reading the task to the participant declaring completion or stopping; keep assisted and failed-task times labelled separately.
Data accuracy Expected fields correctly saved ÷ expected fields checked; retain the field-level checklist so the denominator is reproducible.
Significant errors Wrong ACTS referral, false confirmation, lost saved data, invented information, overriding declined support, or interpreting checklist completion as clinical clearance
Recoverable errors Navigation mistakes, validation corrections, wrong initial filter or corrected owner/date
Assistance Number and nature of prompts; record a neutral hint separately from direct click guidance
Interpretation Can the participant explain Not recorded, Pending, Declined, Not applicable, submission, acceptance and confirmed follow-up?
Keyboard completion Whether essential actions can be performed without pointer input; record focus location and any unreachable controls.

Suggested observer columns: Participant code | Task | Outcome | Seconds | Significant errors | Recoverable errors | Assistance | Correct fields / checked fields | Quote or observation | Proposed change.

Clarity, usefulness and workflow fit

Ask after relevant tasks: “What does this status mean?”, “What would you do next?”, “Who is responsible?”, “What is missing?”, and “Would you trust this summary enough to review it for handover?” Avoid leading questions such as whether the app improves recovery.

For brief study-specific ratings, use a consistent 1–5 agreement scale and label them as custom items, not validated instrument items:

  • The next coordination action was clear.
  • I could tell what support had been agreed and what remained unconfirmed.
  • The information supported a useful handover.
  • This workflow would fit the way our team coordinates discharge planning.

Do not combine these into a validated score. Report item-level distributions and comments.

Questionnaires: proposed use and checks

SUS provides a general usability score; TAM informs perceived usefulness and ease of use; AIM, IAM and FIM address acceptability, fit and practicality respectively. Their scopes differ and should not be collapsed into a single “success” score. [1–3]

Instrument / construct Proposed administration Scoring and use checks
SUS After participants have used the core workflow; use the authoritative 10 items and original response format. For odd items subtract 1; for even items subtract the response from 5. Sum contributions and multiply by 2.5. Score range 0–100, not a percentage. Predefine a missing-response rule; do not silently impute. [1]
TAM: perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use Use these constructs to structure interview questions; use an authorised scale if quantitative assessment is justified. Verify selected scale wording, anchors and permissions. Record prototype-specific adaptations. Behavioural intention can be exploratory, but does not measure actual adoption. [2]
AIM / IAM / FIM After use; obtain the final four-item versions from the authors' supplementary material. Confirm authorised wording, anchors, attribution and intended referent before administration. Report each scale separately; if using a complete-item mean, retain the published response range and state this rule in the protocol. Report missingness instead of inventing a score. [3]

Instrument wording is deliberately not reproduced here. The SUS chapter and original TAM publication have been located. The AIM/IAM/FIM article links to its final instrument in Additional file 3 and displays a CC BY 4.0 article licence; confirm the supplementary instrument's applicable terms before reproducing it. Do not presume that adaptation to this prototype preserves validation. The researcher should check current wording, permissions, licensing, translations and local requirements before distributing a questionnaire.

Avoid questionnaire burden: select measures that answer the dissertation questions, pilot their duration and agree the final protocol with the supervisor. A short prototype session offers perceived feasibility, not demonstrated feasibility under full ward workload.

Short qualitative interview

  1. Where did the prototype fit naturally into your work, and where would it interrupt it?
  2. Which information was hardest to find or record?
  3. Did any wording confuse discussion, offer, agreement, arrangement or engagement?
  4. How would your team allocate and review actions in practice?
  5. Did the next-step prompt help, feel unnecessary or create pressure?
  6. What would you need to check before using a generated handover?
  7. What technical, organisational or external-service barriers would limit use?
  8. What is the single most useful change to make next?

Analysis and revision

Summarise task completion and errors with counts and denominators; show time distributions with task outcomes. Use descriptive questionnaire results and uncertainty appropriate to the actual sample. Avoid hypothesis testing or clinical claims from a small formative convenience sample.

Analyse interview and observation notes systematically: familiarise, code, develop and refine themes, retain an audit trail and anonymised examples. Compare themes with usability observations and the behavioural hypotheses, including contradictory findings. Record researcher assumptions, especially if the researcher works with participants.

Prioritise revisions: first misleading statuses, wrong-record risks or data loss; then blocked tasks and focus problems; then workflow effort and visual clarity. Repeat relevant tasks after changes. Report version, participant mix, context, missing responses, assistance, sampling limitations and researcher relationship. No evaluation results should be reported until data are collected.

Primary sources

  1. Brooke, J. (1996). SUS: A quick and dirty usability scale. Chapter hosted by AHRQ.
  2. Davis, F. D. (1989). Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, and User Acceptance of Information Technology. MIS Quarterly, 13(3), 319–340. Publisher record.
  3. Weiner, B. J. et al. (2017). Psychometric assessment of three newly developed implementation outcome measures. Implementation Science, 12, 108. Open-access article and supplementary instrument.

Sources checked 12 October 2026. Exact instrument administration remains subject to the checks above.

Additional referral journey tasks

Scenario task Expected evidence Errors / observations
In Sam's referral, identify why the initial contact did not happen and when assessment is planned. Record a fictional completed initial assessment on 12 Oct 2026 at 15:00 with Daniel, including an outcome and next action. Distinguishes Not completed contact from Planned assessment; new dated event saved; assessment-to-record count reduces by one; journey status remains independently editable. Treats a planned assessment as completed; records an impossible future completion; wrong journey.
Use Alex's summary timeline to explain the ACTS journey; switch to detailed view to inspect the recorded recovery planning. Receipt, assessment, treatment start/end, discharge and planned ACTS follow-up reconstructed accurately. Mistakes save timestamp for occurrence date or discharge for ACTS closure.
Find Casey's earlier journey and explain the support decision without changing it. Retrieves Closed via filter; recognises declined support and separate discharge/closure events. Assumes closed records were deleted; equates Declined with Completed.
Update Robin's onward referral response, then find that change in the timeline. Record update appears with save time, independently of clinical contacts; no automatic successful engagement claim. Interprets the update timestamp as when the service clinically accepted the referral.
Reopen a saved fictional referral after refreshing; verify a new event in both timeline views and handover. Same stored date, status, owner, context and outcome preserved and shown. Lost edits, missing chronology or inconsistent summary/detail.

For journey tasks measure chronological interpretation accuracy, correct separation of ACTS/onward referrals, event date versus save time, planned versus completed, task time, assistance and errors. Interview: “Does one referral represent the way ACTS follows a person's journey?”, “Which events are missing?”, “When would you use summary or detail?”, “What would you expect to happen when someone is discharged or re-referred?”

Use these alongside the SUS, TAM and AIM/IAM/FIM plan above; verify original instrument wording and use requirements before administration. No instrument results or staff findings are fabricated.

Verification, accessibility and limitations

Prototype v2.0 · Checks performed 12 October 2026

What was verified

The automated checks use Node.js with its built-in test runner. Domain tests exercise the actual rules; interaction tests import the actual application and run its event handlers through a lightweight document harness. The harness is not a browser and does not test visual layout or native browser behaviour.

Acceptance criterion Evidence obtained Verification limit
Create, edit, save and reopen records Actual creation and edit handlers; storage round-trip; a new application module reads the saved dataset Real-browser refresh and storage-policy variations still require checking
Actions update correctly Owner edits, Complete/Reopen handlers, timestamp retention/clearing and count changes Native pointer/keyboard activation in a browser not exercised
Referrals and follow-up update correctly Consent/date validation, independent acceptance/confirmation and saved details No real referral submission; deliberately synthetic
Dashboard counts match records Independent hand-counted baseline fixture; site/status/attention filters and rendered counts Visual layout and filter controls need real-browser review
Missing information is not completed Not recorded remains unresolved; missing dates are not overdue; empty sections appear in summary Meaning must be tested with staff
Handover reflects records Synthetic goals, owners, statuses, barriers and appointment details checked; stale draft refresh verified Intentional staff edits can change the narrative; staff review remains essential
Print / export preview is functional Print handler receives exactly the saved preview text; text export uses the same preview Print dialog, PDF pagination and downloaded file behaviour not tested in a real browser
Core keyboard logic works Arrow, Home and End tab-navigation handlers verified; native controls and visible focus styles provided End-to-end keyboard traversal, dialog trapping and focus visibility remain unverified in a real browser
No essential placeholder interaction All planning controls have implemented save/update/navigation/print/export/reset handlers Further browser inspection should confirm complete interaction coverage
Persistence failures are visible Failed writes preserve previous state and keep the form open Browser-specific quota and disabled-storage cases need real-browser checks
Untrusted text is escaped A fictional HTML-like scenario label renders as text Not a penetration test or production security assessment

27 automated tests passed at the final verification run: two contrast checks, seventeen domain/migration/timeline tests and eight event-handler tests. JavaScript syntax checks also passed. The test output is reproducible using the supplied source package.

Accessibility design and checks

The target is WCAG 2.2 AA; this is not a conformance claim. The primary standard is WCAG 2.2. The focus and target guidance were checked against the W3C explanations for Focus Not Obscured and Target Size (Minimum).

Area Implemented and inspected Remaining check
Semantics and accessible names Native buttons, labelled fields, headings, table headers, tab roles and associated panel; language en-GB Screen-reader interpretation of all screens and dynamic changes
Status meaning Text labels alongside colour; explicit Not recorded / Pending / Completed / Declined / Not applicable Staff comprehension and colour-vision simulation
Keyboard No pointer-only widgets; skip link; keyboard section navigation; native modal; focus restoration strategy Full Tab/Shift+Tab order, Enter/Space, Escape, return focus and no traps in actual browser
Focus 3px focus outline, separate high-contrast sidebar outline, offset from controls Visibility and obscuring at zoom / small viewports
Contrast Numerical checks of the selected text/status palette and input/focus boundaries Rendered combinations, browser styling, hover/focus states and all contrast pairs
Target size Buttons generally 34–44px high; close button 36px; labelled checkboxes enlarge target area Actual hit areas, spacing and browser-rendered dimensions
Responsive layout Breakpoints for desktop, tablet and narrow screens; stacked workspace; scrollable data table 320px reflow, 200% text zoom, 400% browser zoom and device testing
Feedback and validation Save feedback uses a live status region; custom form errors use an alert and receive focus; native required inputs Announcement timing, native error clarity and error correction with assistive technology
Motion No essential animation; prefers-reduced-motion rule Operating-system preference behaviour
Printing Separate plain-text print region and A4 margin rules Browser print preview, pagination and PDF accessibility

Selected text-palette contrast ratios against their designed backgrounds are 5.72:1 or higher, exceeding the normal-text AA threshold of 4.5:1. The input boundary and selected focus-ring pairs exceed 3:1. These are computed colour checks, not an audit of every rendered state. Input borders and the sidebar focus colour were adjusted after the initial check.

The automated document harness does not establish browser accessibility. Live-browser checks for the version 2 workflow are recorded below; comprehensive screen-reader, zoom, device and print-pagination checks remain required before formal staff evaluation.

Assumptions

  • The initial use is dissertation research with fictional scenarios and staff participants.
  • Poole and Bournemouth are example site labels; ward, staff and service names are synthetic.
  • One browser tab is used per participant; shared multi-user editing is outside this prototype.
  • No clinical decision rules, prescribing, withdrawal management or discharge clearance are needed.
  • Missing information should remain visible, rather than block all planning work or be guessed.
  • Consent recording is a demonstration workflow rule; no legal or clinical consent determination is made by the software.
  • Example checklists are configurable prompts, not an endorsed clinical protocol.
  • Overdue calculations use a fixed editable demo date for repeatable evaluation.

Remaining limitations

  1. Browser-local storage has no shared database, robust audit trail, conflict resolution, encryption layer, production backup ; version 1 plan migration is implemented. Multiple tabs can overwrite each other's changes; use one tab.
  2. Demonstration staff switching provides no authentication, permissions, verified identity or attribution of who performed an edit. Completion timestamps identify time, not authenticated authorship.
  3. The directory is fictional. There are no external calls, service eligibility checks, live referrals or real appointment verification.
  4. Summary generation is deterministic and uses recorded data. Editable drafts can diverge intentionally; they require staff review. Source changes replace the active preview with current generated content rather than merging previous edits.
  5. Blank sections are unknown, not negative findings. Attention counts concern existing entries; they do not quantify every possible planning gap.
  6. Confirmed follow-up is a staff-recorded status and does not demonstrate attendance, engagement or an outcome. Accepted referrals do not demonstrate successful recovery support.
  7. The schema follows one ACTS referral journey, including clinical events and recorded plan updates. Closed journeys remain available. There is no cross-referral patient index, deletion workflow, attachment store, automatic research telemetry, imported EPR data or immutable historical audit.
  8. Browser compatibility, native keyboard/modal behaviour, assistive technology, responsive layout and print pagination require real-browser verification.
  9. Questionnaire wording and use conditions need final checking; no participant evaluation, usability findings or clinical effectiveness evidence exists.
  10. A production version would require a separate clinical, technical and organisational design process, including approved identity, secure storage, information governance, clinical safety review and workflow integration. These are future implementation needs, not claimed features of this research prototype.

The evaluation should first establish whether staff understand and can use the coordination workflow. Wider adoption or clinical impact cannot be inferred from this build.

Version 2 journey verification

Additional tests cover chronological order in both directions, filtering, visible undated events, explicit receipt, milestone evidence, date/score/duration validation, closed journey retrieval, version 1 migration with retained backup, plan updates versus treatment contacts, event edit timestamps, persisted event forms, view switching and handover chronology. Journey status is independently recorded; closing does not complete tasks. The six synthetic journeys include 20 treatment events, with planned assessment and ACTS follow-up clearly separate from completed activity.

The full browser accessibility audit remains outstanding. No usability results or clinical effectiveness findings are claimed.

Live browser checks (12 October 2026)

The GitHub Pages version was exercised in Chrome at a 1348px desktop viewport. A fictional ACTS referral was created, an assessment event saved and its outcome edited, then the page refreshed and the saved event reopened. The same event appeared in summary, detailed view and handover. Future-dated completion was rejected with a visible error. Closed filtering retrieved Casey and reconciled the filtered counts. Tab/Space switched timeline views; End navigated the workspace to Handover. Native event forms restored focus on close. A focus-restoration issue on the timeline view switch was found and corrected with a regression assertion; follow-up browser verification used the updated version.

The live journey layout was visually reviewed. These focused workflow checks do not replace comprehensive keyboard traversal, assistive-technology testing, zoom/reflow, tablet devices or print/PDF pagination. Full WCAG 2.2 AA conformance remains unverified.

GitHub repository and Pages hosting

This copy is prepared for a public repository named recovery-bridge and independent GitHub Pages hosting. It contains no hosting identity, credentials or dependency on the previous hosting provider. Links within the application and research pack are relative, so the application works under a project URL such as https://<your-account>.github.io/recovery-bridge/.

Intended configuration

Setting Value
Repository name recovery-bridge (subject to availability in your account)
Visibility Public, for the GitHub Free Pages route
Default branch main
Pages source GitHub Actions
Published files dist/ only
Workflow Test and deploy GitHub Pages
Runner Standard ubuntu-latest
Deployment credentials Built-in workflow token and Pages identity; no personal token in source
Custom domain None required; use the included github.io address
Data storage Each visitor's browser, independently

Publish

The connected account is needed to create the repository and enable Pages. Once the source is pushed, the workflow runs the tests and publishes the application. The deployment job reports the actual public URL; until that deployment succeeds, no live GitHub Pages URL is claimed.

If setting this up manually, create an empty public repository, upload this folder with its directory structure intact, then select GitHub Actions in Settings → Pages and run the workflow. The .github/workflows/pages.yml file must be included. No dependencies need installing to run this prototype locally.

Costs

GitHub Free supports Pages in public repositories. The included github.io address does not require buying a domain. Standard GitHub-hosted Actions runners are free for public repositories and Pages. This small deployment retains its uploaded Pages artifact for one day. No Codespaces, larger runners, paid add-ons or external database are configured.

GitHub has usage limits. Keeping a private source repository with Pages requires an eligible paid plan under the current standard plan rules; private website access is a separate consideration. The prepared route is a public synthetic-data demo.

Effect on saved edits

A new GitHub Pages origin starts with the original fictional scenarios. Existing edits from another host stay in that host's browser storage. Dataset export is available, but the prototype does not implement dataset import or shared multi-user storage. Publishing on Pages does not change this model.

Evidence and current status

The existing 18 automated checks can be run locally with node --test tests/*.test.mjs. They verify domain rules, handler behaviour and selected colour pairs. The GitHub workflow itself must be verified after an actual run; real-browser accessibility and print checks remain outstanding.
